SRINAGAR, Indian-controlled Kashmir (CNN) -- Senior Pakistani and Indian military officials met Tuesday to discuss a border clash in Kashmir, the first major skirmish between South Asia's nuclear rivals since a 2003 cease-fire. Indian army soldiers on the outskirts of Kashmir's summer capital Srinagar. Pakistan's army spokesman Maj. Gen. Athar Abbas told CNN that Pakistan "made our point clear" regarding the firefight, which he said began after Indian soldiers crossed the Line of Control that separates Kashmir between India and Pakistan. But an Indian military spokeswoman, Capt. Neha Goyal, told CNN Pakistani troops crossed the Line of Control and "started firing on our patrol," killing an Indian soldier. "Our troops also retaliated and the Pakistan army troopers ran back," she said. Abbas said "further action should be taken" following Tuesday's "flag meeting," but did not elaborate. The meeting took place along the Line of Control. Reports in India's media said four Pakistani soldiers were killed, but Pakistan's military "strongly denied the report of any (casualties) on the Pakistani side." Pakistan's military also denied its forces crossed the Line of Control, saying the skirmish started when Indian soldiers tried to establish a forward post on Pakistan's side of the line. The firing continued -- intermittently during the whole night." Pakistan said the Indian soldiers "were forced to flee from the area leaving behind their weapons" after the firefight. Indian and Pakistani forces have exchanged periodic gunfire since May, but Monday's clashes appear to be a serious setback to the ongoing peace process between the two nations. India and Pakistan had announced a bilateral cease-fire all along their borders in November 2003 and the cease-fire had been holding on the borders until recently. Kashmir has been at the root of two wars between India and Pakistan, both of which tested nuclear weapons in 1998. India has long accused Pakistan of supporting the separatists in Kashmir, a charge Pakistan denies. India blamed militants from Pakistan for a suicide car bombing outside its embassy in Afghanistan that killed 58 people on July 7. A December 2001 attack on India's parliament that India blamed on the militants brought the two nations to the brink of another war, but they have expanded economic and cultural ties since the November 2003 cease-fire agreement. -- CNN's Aliza Kassim in Atlanta and Mukhtar Ahmad in Srinagar contributed to this report .

Pakistan’s military also denied that its forces crossed the Line of Control, saying the skirmish began when Indian soldiers tried to establish a forward post on Pakistan’s side of the line.

Pakistan said the Indian soldiers “were forced to flee from the area, leaving behind their weapons” after the firefight.

Indian and Pakistani forces have exchanged periodic gunfire since May, but Monday’s clashes appear to represent a serious setback to the ongoing peace process between the two nations.

Kashmir has been at the root of two wars between India and Pakistan, both of which tested nuclear weapons in 1998.

SRINAGAR, Indian-controlled Kashmir (CNN) — High-ranking military representatives from Pakistan and India held talks Tuesday about a clash along the Kashmir border, marking the first significant confrontation between the two nuclear-armed South Asian rivals since a cease-fire was reached in 2003.

Indian army personnel were positioned on the outskirts of Srinagar, the summer capital of Kashmir.

Pakistani army spokesman Maj. Gen. Athar Abbas told CNN that Pakistan had “made our point clear” about the exchange of fire. He said the incident began after Indian troops crossed the Line of Control, the boundary dividing Kashmir between India and Pakistan.

India gave a different account. Capt. Neha Goyal, an Indian military spokeswoman, told CNN that Pakistani soldiers crossed the Line of Control and “started firing on our patrol,” killing one Indian soldier. She said Indian forces returned fire, after which “the Pakistan army troopers ran back.”

Abbas said that “further action should be taken” after Tuesday’s “flag meeting,” but he did not provide details. The meeting was held along the Line of Control.

Indian media reports said four Pakistani soldiers had died in the clash, but Pakistan’s military “strongly denied the report of any casualties on the Pakistani side.”

Pakistan’s military also rejected claims that its troops had crossed the Line of Control. It said the confrontation began when Indian soldiers attempted to set up a forward post on the Pakistani side of the boundary.

“On Pakistan’s objection, Indian troops opened indiscriminate and unprovoked fire,” said a Pakistani military statement released Monday. “The Indian fire was immediately responded to. The firing continued — intermittently during the whole night.”

Pakistan said that after the gun battle, Indian troops “were forced to flee from the area leaving behind their weapons.”

Although Indian and Pakistani forces have traded occasional fire since May, Monday’s fighting appeared to represent a major blow to the peace efforts continuing between the two countries.

India and Pakistan declared a bilateral cease-fire across all their borders in November 2003, and that truce had largely remained in effect until recently.

Kashmir has been the cause of two wars between India and Pakistan, both of which conducted nuclear weapons tests in 1998.

In the Indian-administered part of the mostly Muslim region, an 18-year separatist movement has resulted in more than 43,000 deaths, according to government figures. Human rights organizations and nongovernmental groups estimate the death toll to be about twice as high.

India has repeatedly accused Pakistan of backing separatist fighters in Kashmir, an allegation Pakistan denies.

India also blamed militants from Pakistan for a July 7 suicide car bombing outside its embassy in Afghanistan that killed 58 people.

A December 2001 assault on India’s parliament, which India also attributed to militants, pushed the two countries close to another war. Since the November 2003 cease-fire agreement, however, India and Pakistan have increased their economic and cultural connections.

CNN’s Aliza Kassim in Atlanta and Mukhtar Ahmad in Srinagar contributed to this report.

Senior military officials from India and Pakistan met after a deadly clash along the Line of Control in disputed Kashmir, as both nuclear-armed neighbors traded accusations over who violated a long-standing cease-fire.

The talks involved senior officers responsible for military operations along the heavily militarized frontier, according to officials from both countries. The meeting was aimed at reducing tensions after an exchange of fire that left soldiers dead and raised fears of a broader escalation.

India accused Pakistani forces of initiating the clash and said its troops responded to “unprovoked” firing across the Line of Control, the de facto border dividing Indian- and Pakistani-administered Kashmir. Indian officials said such incidents endanger civilians living near the frontier and undermine efforts to maintain calm.

Pakistan rejected India’s version of events, accusing Indian forces of firing first and violating the cease-fire. Pakistani officials said their military responded only after being targeted, and they called on India to respect existing border agreements.

Both sides said they raised concerns about recent violence and the safety of troops and civilians along the Line of Control. The meeting also focused on using established military communication channels to prevent local clashes from spiraling into larger confrontations.

Kashmir has been a flashpoint between India and Pakistan since the two countries gained independence from Britain in 1947. Both claim the Himalayan region in full but control separate parts of it. The rivals have fought multiple wars over Kashmir, and the Line of Control remains one of the world’s most volatile military frontiers.

India and Pakistan agreed to a cease-fire along the Line of Control in 2003, a deal that significantly reduced cross-border firing for several years. However, both countries have repeatedly accused each other of violating the agreement, especially during periods of heightened political or military tension.

In 2021, the two militaries reaffirmed their commitment to the cease-fire, leading to a notable reduction in violence along the frontier. Still, sporadic clashes, infiltration allegations and competing claims over responsibility continue to strain the fragile arrangement.

The latest meeting signals that both sides are seeking to prevent further escalation, but deep mistrust remains. For civilians living near the Line of Control, even brief breakdowns in the cease-fire can mean evacuation, injury or death.

Indian military officials said Pakistani troops opened “unprovoked” fire late Monday along the Line of Control, the de facto border dividing Indian- and Pakistani-administered Kashmir, targeting forward posts and nearby villages with small arms and mortars. They said Indian forces “responded appropriately.”

A Pakistani military statement rejected that account, accusing Indian troops of initiating the exchange and firing across the line into civilian areas. Pakistani officials said their forces returned fire after what they described as a cease-fire violation by India.

Casualty figures could not be independently verified. Local officials on the Indian-administered side said at least two soldiers and one civilian were killed, while several villagers were wounded and evacuated from settlements close to the frontier. Pakistani authorities reported one soldier killed and accused Indian fire of wounding civilians on their side of the line. Each side disputed the other’s version of events.

Residents in border villages described a night of heavy firing that sent families into bunkers and forced some to leave their homes before dawn. “The shelling started suddenly, and we could hear explosions for hours,” said one resident reached by telephone from a village near the frontier. Schools in some nearby areas were ordered closed as a precaution, local officials said.

The Line of Control has been the scene of frequent skirmishes despite the cease-fire announced by India and Pakistan in November 2003. That agreement significantly reduced violence along the frontier for several years, allowing limited cross-border travel and trade to resume. But both countries have accused each other of repeated violations, particularly during periods of heightened political tension or militant attacks.

India says Pakistan supports and arms militants who cross the Line of Control to carry out attacks in Indian-administered Kashmir, an allegation Islamabad denies. Pakistan says it provides only diplomatic and moral support to Kashmiris seeking self-determination and accuses India of using excessive force in the region.

Kashmir has been at the center of the India-Pakistan rivalry since the two countries gained independence from British rule in 1947. Both claim the Himalayan territory in full but control separate portions of it. The dispute has sparked two of the three major wars fought between the nuclear-armed neighbors and has remained one of the world’s most volatile territorial conflicts.

Tensions intensified after an armed insurgency erupted in Indian-administered Kashmir in 1989, leading to decades of violence involving militants, Indian security forces and civilians. India has maintained a large security presence in the region, while Pakistan has repeatedly called for international mediation. New Delhi insists the dispute must be handled bilaterally.

The latest exchange comes amid limited diplomatic contact between the two governments. Military commanders from both sides have used hotline communications in the past to contain frontier incidents, but officials did not immediately say whether such contact had taken place after Monday’s firing.

Analysts said even brief border clashes can carry broader risks because of the history of escalation between the two countries.

“Cease-fire violations along the Line of Control are not new, but the danger is always that a localized incident becomes politically charged,” said a Srinagar-based political analyst. “Both sides tend to frame these incidents in sharply different ways, and that makes de-escalation harder.”

By Tuesday afternoon, firing had subsided in the affected sector, according to local officials, though troops on both sides remained on alert. Villagers said they feared renewed shelling after nightfall.

**Firefight Along Kashmir Frontier Strains India-Pakistan Peace Efforts**

*By [Reporter Name]*  
*[Dateline], [Day]*

A firefight along the Line of Control dividing Indian- and Pakistani-administered Kashmir on Monday has raised fresh concerns over the fragile peace process between the two nuclear-armed neighbors, even as military officials from both sides held a flag meeting to prevent the incident from escalating.

Indian and Pakistani officials offered differing accounts of the exchange, which occurred along the heavily militarized frontier that separates the two sides of the disputed Himalayan region. Each side accused the other of violating ceasefire understandings, a familiar pattern in the decades-long conflict over Kashmir.

Following the incident, local military commanders met under a white flag at a designated crossing point along the Line of Control. Such meetings are routinely used to defuse tensions, exchange complaints and seek assurances that firing will not spread to other sectors.

Officials said the talks focused on restoring calm, maintaining communication between field commanders and avoiding further escalation. No immediate breakthrough was announced, but both sides appeared to signal an interest in containing the confrontation.

The Line of Control has been one of the world’s most volatile military frontiers since it was established after the 1971 India-Pakistan war. Although a ceasefire agreement reached in 2003 significantly reduced cross-border firing for years, periodic clashes have continued to disrupt civilian life in border villages and unsettle diplomatic engagement.

Monday’s incident comes at a sensitive moment for India-Pakistan relations. Any exchange of fire along the frontier can quickly become politically charged, especially when it involves allegations of infiltration, militant activity or civilian casualties. Domestic pressure in both countries often narrows the space for compromise, making it harder for leaders to sustain dialogue.

Analysts say the clash threatens the peace process for three main reasons. First, violence along the Line of Control undermines trust between the two militaries, whose cooperation is essential for maintaining calm. Second, it gives political opponents and hard-line groups on both sides an opportunity to argue against engagement. Third, it risks linking security incidents to broader diplomatic talks, causing negotiations on trade, travel, prisoners or humanitarian measures to stall.

Kashmir remains at the heart of the India-Pakistan dispute. Both countries claim the region in full but control separate portions of it. The dispute has triggered multiple wars and repeated crises, and it continues to shape military deployments and diplomatic relations across South Asia.

The flag meeting suggests both sides are attempting to manage the fallout from Monday’s firefight. But the episode highlights how quickly localized violence along the frontier can threaten wider efforts to stabilize relations between New Delhi and Islamabad.

For civilians living near the Line of Control, the immediate concern is whether the calm will hold. For diplomats, the larger question is whether the peace process can survive another test from the region’s most dangerous flashpoint.

## Pakistan and India trade accusations after reported Kashmir border clash

**Srinagar, Indian-administered Kashmir** — Indian and Pakistani forces exchanged fire along the heavily militarized frontier in Kashmir, according to officials and local media reports, in an incident that has again raised tensions between the nuclear-armed neighbors.

The reported clash took place near the Line of Control, the de facto border dividing Indian- and Pakistani-administered Kashmir. Both militaries issued statements denying responsibility for initiating the confrontation and accused the other side of violating ceasefire understandings.

India’s military said Pakistani troops opened “unprovoked” fire on forward positions, prompting what it called a “calibrated and effective response.” Pakistan’s military rejected that account, saying Indian forces had targeted positions and nearby civilian areas first. Neither side provided independently verifiable evidence, and access to the frontier area remains tightly restricted.

Local media on both sides reported casualties, though the numbers could not be independently confirmed. Indian outlets cited defense sources as saying that several soldiers may have been injured in the exchange. Pakistani media, citing security officials and local administrators, reported that civilians in villages near the frontier had been wounded by shelling. In previous incidents along the Line of Control, both governments have often disputed each other’s casualty claims.

The latest reported clash comes despite a 2021 recommitment by India and Pakistan to observe a ceasefire along the Line of Control, an agreement that significantly reduced cross-border firing after years of frequent exchanges. However, both countries continue to accuse each other of provocations, infiltration attempts and support for hostile activity in Kashmir.

Kashmir, a Himalayan region claimed in full by both India and Pakistan and controlled in part by each, has been one of the world’s most volatile flashpoints since the two countries gained independence from Britain in 1947. They have fought multiple wars over the territory, and the region remains heavily militarized.

India has long accused Pakistan of supporting armed groups that operate in Indian-administered Kashmir. Pakistan denies giving military support to militants and says it provides diplomatic and moral support to Kashmiris seeking self-determination. New Delhi rejects that characterization, saying the violence is driven by Pakistan-backed terrorism.

Separatist violence in Indian-administered Kashmir has declined from the peaks of the 1990s and early 2000s, when insurgency-related deaths numbered in the thousands annually. Indian government data in recent years has pointed to a sharp reduction in militant attacks, security-force casualties and civilian deaths, though rights groups say the region remains under heavy security restrictions and that political grievances persist. Analysts note that while violence levels have fallen, sporadic militant attacks, targeted killings and clashes between armed groups and security forces continue.

In 2001, an attack on the Indian Parliament brought the two countries to the brink of war; India blamed groups including Jaish-e-Mohammed and Lashkar-e-Taiba. In 2019, a suicide bombing in Pulwama killed 40 Indian paramilitary personnel; Jaish-e-Mohammed claimed responsibility, and India later carried out airstrikes in Pakistan’s Balakot area, triggering aerial clashes between the two countries.

Pakistan has consistently denied state involvement in such attacks and has accused India of using security incidents to deflect attention from conditions inside Indian-administered Kashmir. India says Pakistan has failed to dismantle militant infrastructure on its soil.

The latest border incident also comes against the backdrop of continuing political tension in Kashmir. In 2019, India revoked the region’s semi-autonomous status and split the former state of Jammu and Kashmir into federally administered territories, a move Pakistan condemned as illegal. India said the decision was necessary to integrate the region more fully and improve governance and development.

Diplomatic ties between New Delhi and Islamabad remain limited, and direct dialogue has been largely frozen for years. Analysts say even relatively small border clashes can carry outsized risks because of the history of rapid escalation between the two rivals.

For residents living near the Line of Control, the fear is immediate. Villages on both sides have in the past been evacuated during intense shelling, with schools closed and families moving into bunkers or safer areas. Local officials have often called for restraint, saying civilians bear the brunt when ceasefire violations spiral.
